steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on event collapse in contrast maximization frameworks for event cameras. Introduce event cameras and contrast maximization, explain what event collapse is and why it deserves a proper study, sketch our approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Event cameras and the contrast maximization (CMax) framework
2. Event alignment and the event collapse problem
3. Our approach: collapse even in 1-DOF motion; principled metrics as penalties
4. Contributions
5. Closing statement on novelty and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Event cameras and CMax
- advantages over standard cameras in difficult scenarios: high speed, high dynamic range, low power
- unconventional data: per-pixel asynchronous brightness changes (events) -> new algorithms needed to unlock advantages
- CMax: event processing framework, state-of-the-art on many tasks
- tasks: rotational motion estimation; feature flow estimation and tracking; ego-motion estimation; 3D reconstruction; optical flow estimation; motion segmentation; guided filtering; image reconstruction

2. Event collapse
- CMax and similar event alignment frameworks: find motion and/or scene parameters aligning corresponding events (triggered by same scene edge) -> motion compensation
- simultaneously estimates motion parameters and correspondences (data association)
- sometimes converges to undesired solution: events accumulate into too few pixels = event collapse (Figure 1)
- CMax at heart of many state-of-the-art event-based motion estimation methods -> must understand limitation, find ways to overcome
- prior works: largely ignored, or workarounds without detailed analysis
- thorough discussion overdue = goal of this work

3. Our approach
- expectation: collapse when event transformation sufficiently complex; we show it may occur even for one degree-of-freedom (DOF) motion
- inspiration: differential geometry, electrostatics
- principled metrics to quantify collapse; penalty terms in event alignment objective
- collapse depends on many factors; modify objective's landscape -> better well-posedness, use standard optimization algorithms

4. Contributions
- study of event collapse w.r.t. event warping and objective functions (Sections 3.3 and 4)
- two principled metrics (flow divergence; area-element deformations) used as regularizers (Sections 3.4 to 3.6)
- experiments on publicly available datasets, comparison with other strategies (Section 4)

5. Closing
- first work focusing on event collapse, which may arise in state-of-the-art event-alignment methods
- metrics mitigate collapse without harming well-posed warps

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Event cameras have potential advantages over standard cameras for difficult scenarios (high speed, high dynamic range, low power). But they produce an unconventional type of data (per-pixel asynchronous brightness changes, called events), and new algorithms are needed to deal with this data and unlock their advantages. Contrast maximization (CMax) is an event processing framework that gives state-of-the-art results on several tasks, like rotational motion estimation, feature flow estimation and tracking, ego-motion estimation, 3D reconstruction, optical flow estimation, motion segmentation, guided filtering, and image reconstruction.

The main idea of CMax and of similar event alignment frameworks is to find the motion and/or scene parameters that align corresponding events (i.e. events that are triggered by the same scene edge), and in this way achieve motion compensation. The framework estimates the motion parameters and the correspondences between events (data association) at the same time. But in some cases the CMax optimization converges to an undesired solution where the events accumulate into too few pixels. This phenomenon is called event collapse (Figure 1). Since CMax is at the heart of many state-of-the-art event-based motion estimation methods, it is important to understand this limitation and to propose ways to overcome it. Prior works have mostly ignored the issue, or they proposed workarounds without analyzing the phenomenon in detail. A more thorough discussion of the phenomenon is overdue, and this is the goal of this work.

3. Our approach
- expectation: collapse when event transformation sufficiently complex; we show it may occur even for one degree-of-freedom (DOF) motion
- inspiration: differential geometry, electrostatics
- principled metrics to quantify collapse; penalty terms in event alignment objective
- collapse depends on many factors; modify objective's landscape -> better well-posedness, use standard optimization algorithms

4. Contributions
- study of event collapse w.r.t. event warping and objective functions (Sections 3.3 and 4)
- two principled metrics (flow divergence; area-element deformations) used as regularizers (Sections 3.4 to 3.6)
- experiments on publicly available datasets, comparison with other strategies (Section 4)

5. Closing
- first work focusing on event collapse, which may arise in state-of-the-art event-alignment methods
- metrics mitigate collapse without harming well-posed warps

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Event cameras have potential advantages over standard cameras for difficult scenarios (high speed, high dynamic range, low power). But they produce an unconventional type of data (per-pixel asynchronous brightness changes, called events), and new algorithms are needed to deal with this data and unlock their advantages. Contrast maximization (CMax) is an event processing framework that gives state-of-the-art results on several tasks, like rotational motion estimation, feature flow estimation and tracking, ego-motion estimation, 3D reconstruction, optical flow estimation, motion segmentation, guided filtering, and image reconstruction.

The main idea of CMax and of similar event alignment frameworks is to find the motion and/or scene parameters that align corresponding events (i.e. events that are triggered by the same scene edge), and in this way achieve motion compensation. The framework estimates the motion parameters and the correspondences between events (data association) at the same time. But in some cases the CMax optimization converges to an undesired solution where the events accumulate into too few pixels. This phenomenon is called event collapse (Figure 1). Since CMax is at the heart of many state-of-the-art event-based motion estimation methods, it is important to understand this limitation and to propose ways to overcome it. Prior works have mostly ignored the issue, or they proposed workarounds without analyzing the phenomenon in detail. A more thorough discussion of the phenomenon is overdue, and this is the goal of this work.

It is expected that event collapse happens when the event transformation becomes complex enough, but we show that it can happen even in the simplest case of one degree-of-freedom (DOF) motion. We take inspiration from differential geometry and electrostatics and propose principled metrics to quantify event collapse, and we discourage it by adding penalty terms to the event alignment objective function. Event collapse depends on many factors, but our strategy aims at modifying the landscape of the objective to improve the well-posedness of the problem and to be able to use well-known, standard optimization algorithms.

In summary, our contributions are:

- 1. A study of the event collapse phenomenon with regard to event warping and objective functions (Sections 3.3 and 4).

- 2. Two principled metrics of event collapse (one based on flow divergence and one based on area-element deformations) and their use as regularizers to mitigate the phenomenon (Sections 3.4 to 3.6).

- 3. Experiments on publicly available datasets that show the effectiveness of the proposed regularizers, compared with other strategies (Section 4).

As far as we know, this is the first work that focuses on the paramount phenomenon of event collapse, which may arise in state-of-the-art event-alignment methods. Our experiments show that the proposed metrics mitigate event collapse and that they do not harm well-posed warps.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Event cameras [1,2,3] offer potential advantages over standard cameras for tackling difficult scenarios (high speed, high dynamic range, low power). However, new algorithms are needed to deal with the unconventional type of data they produce (per-pixel asynchronous brightness changes, called events) and to unlock their advantages [4]. Contrast maximization (CMax) is an event processing framework that provides state-of-the-art results on several tasks, such as rotational motion estimation [5,6], feature flow estimation and tracking [7,8,9,10,11], ego-motion estimation [12,13,14], 3D reconstruction [12,15], optical flow estimation [16,17,18,19], motion segmentation [20,21,22,23,24], guided filtering [25], and image reconstruction [26].

The main idea of CMax and similar event alignment frameworks [27,28] is to find the motion and/or scene parameters that align corresponding events (i.e., events triggered by the same scene edge), thus achieving motion compensation. The framework simultaneously estimates the motion parameters and the correspondences between events (data association). However, in some cases the CMax optimization converges to an undesired solution where events accumulate into too few pixels, a phenomenon called event collapse (Figure 1). Because CMax is at the heart of many state-of-the-art event-based motion estimation methods, it is important to understand this limitation and propose ways to overcome it. Prior works have largely ignored the issue or proposed workarounds without analyzing the phenomenon in detail. A more thorough discussion of the phenomenon is overdue, and this is the goal of this work.

Contrary to the expectation that event collapse occurs when the event transformation becomes sufficiently complex [16,27], we show that it may occur even in the simplest case of one degree-of-freedom (DOF) motion. Drawing inspiration from differential geometry and electrostatics, we propose principled metrics to quantify event collapse and discourage it by adding penalty terms to the event alignment objective function. Although event collapse depends on many factors, our strategy aims at modifying the objective's landscape to improve the well-posedness of the problem and to be able to use well-known, standard optimization algorithms.

In summary, our contributions are:

- 1. A study of the event collapse phenomenon with regard to event warping and objective functions (Sections 3.3 and 4).

- 2. Two principled metrics of event collapse (one based on flow divergence and one based on area-element deformations) and their use as regularizers to mitigate the above-mentioned phenomenon (Sections 3.4 to 3.6).

- 3. Experiments on publicly available datasets that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed regularizers in comparison with other strategies (Section 4).

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that focuses on the paramount phenomenon of event collapse, which may arise in state-of-the-art event-alignment methods. Our experiments show that the proposed metrics mitigate event collapse without harming well-posed warps.
